items.statement: Fentanyl test strips do not show other drugs, such as xylazine.
items.why: This is one of the strips' known limits, along with some people misreading them.

items.statement: Sleep-lab studies found cannabis taken by mouth helps people fall asleep faster.
items.why: Time to fall asleep did not change compared with a dummy pill. Most tested CBD or mild THC medicines; smoking was not tested.

items.statement: Mild serotonin syndrome is easy to tell apart from ordinary drug effects.
items.why: Mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects; doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever. A checklist of these signs was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses.

items.statement: Caffeine makes people who rarely have it more alert.
items.why: In one lab study, caffeine made them faster but raised their jitters, not their alertness. It's one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits.

items.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
items.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, and the data cover only the first week after stopping, so how long it lasts isn't known.

items.statement: After MDMA in a sleep lab, dreaming (REM) sleep almost disappeared that night, then came back the next night.
items.why: A short night without MDMA did not remove dreaming sleep this way, in this study of 7 people.

items.statement: If an antidepressant mutes MDMA's effects, that means less MDMA is in your blood.
items.why: In small trials, two antidepressants lowered how strongly people rated MDMA's effects, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher. That's second-hand, from single trials of 16 healthy people each.

items.statement: In a 3-day test, men who drink coffee daily peed much more on coffee days than on water days.
items.why: They peed about the same: 2.41 litres a day on coffee days, 2.43 on water days. One test, 50 men used to coffee.

items.statement: In published cases of repeated vomiting with regular cannabis use, most people found hot baths or showers eased it for a while.
items.why: Most of the 211 people in published cases found this. But many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.

items.statement: Most people throw their drugs away when a fentanyl test strip shows fentanyl.
items.why: Few do. At a supervised injection site, people said they would throw it away after only 11 in 100 checks showing fentanyl.

items.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.
items.why: After the laws, deaths ran about 7 in 100 below the expected trend, but the study didn't check whether more people used strips, and the drop came in each law's very first month. Other changes at the same time could explain it.

items.statement: Thinking you've drunk alcohol, when you haven't, is enough to change your mood and memory.
items.why: Across 36 experiments, the belief went with more drinking but not mood or memory changes; the alcohol itself affected those.

items.statement: In trials where people did not know which pill they got, disulfiram, a medicine for drinking problems, showed no clear benefit.
items.why: Disulfiram showed no clear benefit in these trials, but none tested taking it with someone watching, which may make it look less helpful.

items.statement: Bupropion and modafinil have been shown to help people stop using meth.
items.why: Across five trials, about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, whether on medicine or a dummy pill. The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.

items.statement: In a Johns Hopkins psilocybin study, fewer than 5 in 100 volunteers felt strong fear.
items.why: No: 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

items.statement: You can't become dependent on cannabis, even if you use it every day.
items.why: Reviews give figures from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2 for people who use daily, though none can show what causes what.

items.statement: MDMA has been tried in couples therapy for PTSD, and both partners felt happier together afterwards.
items.why: Two small studies, 14 couples in all. Neither had a group without MDMA, and this couples therapy helps PTSD even without it.

items.statement: Some people who took very large amounts of loperamide (Imodium) got serious heart-rhythm problems.
items.why: Some needed a breathing tube or a pacemaker. Poisons doctors tend to see sicker cases, so the study cannot show how often this happens.

items.statement: In studies that looked for problems after psychedelics like psilocybin or LSD, severe anxiety was the most common.
items.why: Headaches were the most common; one person had a severe worsening of anxiety. Most studies were in labs or ceremonies with support.

items.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.
items.why: One 2007 review ranked MAOI antidepressants highest and SSRI-type antidepressants lower. That's the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work; no study counted how often each mix causes harm.

items.statement: In Maryland, death certificates named heroin in almost every death a fuller review linked to heroin.
items.why: They named it in only about 52 in 100. Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.

items.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
items.why: It depends how you count: an old US survey found about 11 in 100 had ever been dependent, and a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years. Neither had a number for meth alone.

items.statement: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart and fast breathing.
items.why: The body can also overheat, chest pain can happen, and some people lose touch with reality. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

items.statement: A computer model gave cannabis no effect at all. Yet people in it still mostly used cannabis first.
items.why: Some people were likelier to use any drug and were offered cannabis first. So cannabis coming first does not prove it leads on.

items.statement: In one study, daily use of strong cannabis went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis.
items.why: That's compared with never using, in 11 places in Europe and Brazil. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times, and the gap between strong and weaker could be chance.

items.statement: Meth comes in two mirror-image forms, and which form it is depends on how it was made.
items.why: In one small study of 12 men, the two forms acted differently: the 'l' form raised blood pressure less.

items.statement: Psilocybin has been shown to help people quit smoking.
items.why: In one small study, 12 of just 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later. With no comparison group, no one can tell what psilocybin added.

items.statement: In one study, people who used meth already had lower school grades from before they started.
items.why: Their adult scores were also lower than those grades predicted. Nobody took these tests before they started using.

items.statement: Among emergency patients who'd taken GHB or GBL, those who'd also had alcohol more often went to critical care.
items.why: Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts weren't known.

items.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.
items.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to it, and tests after death found none in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one doesn't prove cause.

items.statement: In one study, a few ecstasy pills did not change a serotonin marker in young people scanned before and after.
items.why: Scanned before and about 17 months later, the marker had not changed. But most had taken only one or two pills in all.

items.statement: Alcohol is listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
items.why: Death certificates have listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008, and more often for men than women. Alcohol is often left off death records, and counts like these can't say how much it adds to risk.

items.statement: Soon after THC, the main active part of cannabis, people did just as well on lab driving tests as after a dummy.
items.why: In 80 pooled lab studies, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after a dummy.

items.statement: People with regular or problematic meth or amphetamine use died nearly 7 times as often as others their age.
items.why: That's about 1 in 90 a year, in studies of people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids, so not all of it is the drug.

items.statement: Taking benzodiazepines for a long time has been shown to cause dementia.
items.why: Not shown: neither of two studies could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions. Quebec records linked long use to Alzheimer's, but a Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

items.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.
items.why: By 12 weeks, the gap between the full dose and a tiny dose could be chance, though the full dose did better at 3 weeks. Everyone in that trial of 233 adults got some psilocybin, so it compared doses.

items.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
items.why: One review describes two studies of people on methadone: their tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

items.statement: A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after alcohol withdrawal begins.
items.why: The review describes the DTs as fast-coming confusion with withdrawal signs, usually lasting 2 or 3 days.

items.statement: A US survey found tobacco hooked a bigger share of people who'd used it than cocaine or meth-like stimulants.
items.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, stimulants other than cocaine about 11, in an early-1990s survey that included people who'd only just started. A broader Australian count, done differently, estimated about 50 in 100 for stimulants within 14 years of starting.

items.statement: In one study, fentanyl withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, unlike heroin-type withdrawal.
items.why: The other group's withdrawal eased from the start, but the two groups were studied ten years apart.

items.statement: In the one year-long study of fentanyl test strips, recent strip use rose between the start and the end.
items.why: Recent strip use fell by the end. More had ever tried a strip, among those who answered all three surveys. Many people left the study.

items.statement: At one English festival, drug-related hospital cases fell from 19 to 1 the year on-site testing began.
items.why: Drug cases went from 19 in 2015 to 1 in 2016, but other hospital admissions rose from 40 to 49, and no festival was compared.

items.statement: Studies have compared people given fentanyl test strips with people not given them, to see what strips change.
items.why: No study has. What we know comes from what people said they did; nobody watched what they actually did.

items.statement: In old trials, benzodiazepines made seizures during alcohol withdrawal much rarer.
items.why: About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills, and delirium was less common too. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.

items.statement: In one study, people dependent on meth reported more violent crime in months they used it.
items.why: It was about 12 in 100 months with meth use, against 3 in 100 without, comparing each person with themselves. But use and crime were reported for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

items.statement: If a drug is found in someone's body after death, that shows the drug caused the death.
items.why: Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death, and one death can be counted under several drugs.

items.statement: UK experts judged legal alcohol and tobacco less harmful than LSD and ecstasy.
items.why: The reverse: experts ranked alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy in 2007, and alcohol top overall in 2010. These are expert opinions, not measurements.

items.statement: Two big trials comparing ketamine drips with ECT for depression came to the same answer.
items.why: No: a US trial found ketamine at least as good; in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.

items.statement: Family members only feel better if their loved one starts treatment.
items.why: In one trial, family members felt less depressed and angry in every group, whether or not the relative started treatment. With no group left without help, no approach can take the credit.

items.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.
items.why: In the first survey, that was fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol. The surveys ran from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition; newer US figures that count milder cases are higher.

items.statement: In a global study, alcohol was the top risk factor for death among people aged 15 to 49.
items.why: The Global Burden of Disease study put about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women at those ages down to alcohol. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

items.statement: In US hospitals, most people with chest pain after cocaine were having a heart attack.
items.why: About 1 to 6 in 100 were, in 1990s studies whose blood tests could miss small heart attacks.

items.statement: Esketamine nasal spray passed its main test in both of its big 4-week trials.
items.why: Only one of the two passed. In both, depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine.

items.statement: Most people on acamprosate in trials still drank again during treatment.
items.why: About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills, and the most carefully run trials found no clear difference. Most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker.

items.statement: In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used nitrous oxide (laughing gas) in the past year reported lasting numbness.
items.why: 200 of 4,633 said so. But no doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common this is.

items.statement: In one experiment, describing a person's trouble as 'drug use', not a 'health concern', made readers see them as more dangerous.
items.why: Readers also wanted more distance from the person. They rated made-up stories; no one checked how people are really treated.

items.statement: In a US trial, people got one psilocybin session or a vitamin pill. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin.
items.why: Over 6 weeks, in 104 adults. But people could probably tell they had psilocybin, and nobody checked.

items.statement: Kids who had the original DARE classes went on to use less alcohol, tobacco and drugs than other kids.
items.why: Across 11 studies, they used them about as much as other kids. Only DARE before its 2001 rebuild was tested.

items.statement: In UK deaths linked to ketamine, other drugs were always found too.
items.why: From 1993 to 2006, ketamine was the only drug found in 4 of 23 deaths. Finding it does not show it caused them.

items.statement: In 1990s New York, cocaine overdose deaths were more common on hot days.
items.why: 2.34 deaths a day on hot days against 1.76 on other days, but the study compared days, not people.

items.statement: In one study, brothers and sisters without drug problems shared some brain differences with their sibling dependent on stimulants.
items.why: This suggests some may run in families, though 94 in 100 of the dependent siblings were dependent on cocaine.

items.statement: In many alcohol studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill.
items.why: People who had stopped died more often; against people who never drank, those drinking a little showed no clear difference.

items.statement: Brain studies agree that meth use shrinks the brain.
items.why: Some studies found smaller brain areas soon after stopping, but others found some areas larger.

items.statement: The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.
items.why: The drug came from a wrongly labelled bottle, and the study was withdrawn a year later. The withdrawal notice doesn't say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

items.statement: When 96 in 100 people given naloxone for an opioid overdose survive, naloxone saved 96 lives in 100.
items.why: False. Most opioid overdoses don't end in death, so survival can't count lives saved.

items.statement: In a lab test, people rated LSD and psilocybin trips much alike.
items.why: In 28 people, the ratings barely differed. But that's no proof they're the same, and most could tell which drug they'd had.

items.statement: In several studies, people who said they slept badly soon after stopping heavy drinking were more likely to drink again.
items.why: Long heavy drinking can leave sleep poor for months. This comes second-hand from a review that did not check study quality.

items.statement: Naltrexone helped less, if at all, with stopping drinking completely.
items.why: Trials found its benefit in heavy drinking: about 46 in 100 went back to it, against 54 on dummy pills.

items.statement: People with no working version of the enzyme that clears MDMA get far higher levels of it.
items.why: Their peak level was only about 15 percent higher, and only in the first 3 hours: MDMA seems to switch that enzyme off itself, so these body differences matter less. Just 7 such people were studied.

items.statement: Slowly cutting down methadone took away all the aches, bad sleep and worry of withdrawal.
items.why: Neither way seemed to remove all of these symptoms, whether methadone or clonidine-type medicines.

items.statement: In a big review, more drinking went with more breast cancer, as well as mouth, throat and liver cancer.
items.why: Breast cancer was about 1.6 times as common at more than four drinks a day, against not drinking.

items.statement: In gene studies, drinking more went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
items.why: In a big study of Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and bleeding strokes rose most. Women, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes.

items.statement: A bad reaction to PCP always wears off within about a day.
items.why: In three cases reported in 1975, a severe breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP lasted two to four weeks, then passed. Only three cases, and nobody tested the drugs they'd taken.

items.statement: At one US autopsy centre, deaths nobody thought were from drugs almost never turned out to be drug deaths.
items.why: Drug tests showed about 49 in 100 of the 237 deaths nobody thought were from drugs actually were, and about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause. Only two US places have been studied, so others may differ.

items.statement: In studies of ecstasy, almost everyone also used cannabis.
items.why: 90 to 100 in 100 did, so a study of ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once.

items.statement: A negative xylazine test strip means there's no xylazine.
items.why: With less xylazine than strips are made to find, only 6 of 28 samples read positive, against 37 of 38 with at least that much. That was one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment.

items.statement: In lab studies, people who felt anxious just before taking LSD had more anxiety during the session.
items.why: This held in 213 healthy adults in a hospital room; the paper gives the link's direction, not its size.

items.statement: In lab choice tests, people who use meth almost always chose the drug over small amounts of cash.
items.why: They often chose cash, picking the drug about 4 times in 10 in one group, fewer than 2 in 10 in another. Only 13 men.

items.statement: People who had their first drink at 14 or younger more often had alcohol dependence than late starters.
items.why: In a big US survey, about 4 to 5 in 10 who started at 14 or younger had been dependent at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. But people had to remember their first drink, and some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.

items.statement: In two small studies, people felt much sadder the day after ecstasy than others did.
items.why: People felt very tired and had slept less, but their next-day mood was about the same as others'.

items.statement: When meth's good feelings fade over days of use, the bad effects fade too.
items.why: In a small lab study, the good feelings were gone within three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew and appetite stayed down. Only six to nine people took part, on small doses.

items.statement: In a lab study, people's thinking was clearly worse the day after LSD.
items.why: In 24 people, a few memory and word tests went a little better the next morning and one rule-switching puzzle a little worse, which may just be chance. The report gave no mood or sleep data.

items.statement: In death records from 27 US states, most deaths where kratom was named as a cause had no other drug found.
items.why: Only 7 of 91 had kratom alone; other drugs turned up in the rest, and fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.

items.statement: In British Columbia in 2016 and 2017, about 7 in 10 people who died of a drug overdose were using alone.
items.why: Coroners' reports, cited by a survey, found this. On its own, it cannot show whether using alone changes overdose risk.

items.statement: In doctors' reports of health problems after laughing gas, most people had numbness or tingling.
items.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

items.statement: The day after some benzo sleeping pills, people drove worse than with alcohol at a common drink-driving limit.
items.why: In tests in a real car or a driving machine, weaving inside the lane was worse with some pills than with alcohol at the limit used in several countries. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.

items.statement: In one big survey, people sought emergency treatment more often after LSD than after magic mushrooms.
items.why: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year said they had, mostly for panic, anxiety or confusion, against 2 in 1,000 after magic mushrooms. Nobody checked the answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.

items.statement: In a lab study, MDA brought more visions than MDMA, but less anxiety.
items.why: That's what 12 people on MDA reported, set against MDMA results from other people in earlier studies, so it's a weak comparison.

items.statement: Clonidine and lofexidine barely help with heroin withdrawal.
items.why: In three trials, about 19 in 100 on them had bad withdrawal, against about 59 in 100 on a dummy pill, and more finished treatment. But the trials were small and old, and none included people coming off fentanyl.

items.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
items.why: Combining three studies on thoughts and three on attempts, a review found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

items.statement: In one small study, most symptoms of stopping meth eased within one to two weeks.
items.why: On a hospital research ward, most reported symptoms eased in that time, though low mood and craving lasted longer.

items.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, cases that also named an antidepressant more often ended in death.
items.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

items.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.
items.why: About 47 in 100 on a cannabis medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on a dummy. But only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials in the review had serious weaknesses.

items.statement: It's been shown in people that using in a new place makes an overdose more likely.
items.why: In people there's only one study: 10 overdose survivors' memories, with nobody to compare them with. In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place.

items.statement: In a lab psilocybin study, fewer than 1 in 20 volunteers felt strong fear.
items.why: 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point.

items.statement: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look so alike that no symptom has been shown to reliably tell them apart.
items.why: Hallucinations and delusions were not clearly different in 12 small studies; flatness and withdrawal were somewhat milder in meth psychosis.

items.statement: About 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths at one US autopsy centre had another cause, like a blood clot in the lungs.
items.why: Full autopsies and drug tests showed it; in some, no drug was found at all. Only two US places have been studied.

items.statement: It's proven that trip tunnels and spirals come from the brain's wiring.
items.why: A maths model suggests it, but it wasn't tested in people on a drug.

items.statement: In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent three years later.
items.why: Some still had a few signs, and numbers depend on who is counted. Many who recovered from alcohol problems were never treated.

items.statement: In the 1978 Rat Park study, rats living together refused morphine water.
items.why: They drank it, and when it was almost all they had, they drank more than rats kept alone. All of this was in rats.

items.statement: Trials show that CBD oil from a shop cuts seizures in children with a severe epilepsy.
items.why: Not shown: the trials tested a drug company's CBD medicine. CBD products from shops were not tested.

items.statement: In lab studies, meth made attention and memory clearly worse at the time.
items.why: In small lab studies, attention, memory and reaction time didn't get measurably worse. But small or moderate harm can't be ruled out, and binges weren't tested.

items.statement: Benzo withdrawal can feel like the anxiety or sleep problems the pills were for.
items.why: The reviews say withdrawal symptoms can feel like the original problem. They're expert reviews, not studies, so this is second-hand.

items.statement: Headaches from skipping caffeine come from expecting them, not from the missing caffeine.
items.why: Off their usual caffeine before a small operation, 10 of 20 people on dummy pills had a headache by evening and none of 20 on caffeine pills did, and neither they nor the doctor checking knew who got which. Only 40 patients took part, though, and surgery can also cause headaches.

items.statement: In one US study, most one-dollar bills had traces of cocaine.
items.why: About 9 in 10 did, typically a little over a millionth of a gram. But it was 50 bills collected by 2000.

items.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.
items.why: A big review found small gaps in learning, memory, attention and planning, but none clear for language, shape or movement. People were tested only after they'd started, so it can't show cannabis caused the gap.

items.statement: A review of how ketamine works says nobody knows how much of it reaches the human brain.
items.why: So a lot of what we know about how it works comes from animals and from cells in dishes.

items.statement: Most US soldiers who were hooked on narcotics in Vietnam stayed hooked after coming home.
items.why: About 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics in Vietnam, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

items.statement: In studies, death rates were highest in the first weeks after leaving methadone.
items.why: In 5 studies, deaths in the first 4 weeks off methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on. People who leave may differ in other ways.

items.statement: In a lab, people given cocaine felt less hot in a heated suit, even though their bodies warmed up more.
items.why: They began to sweat later and warmed up more than after a comparison drug, yet felt less hot. Only 7 people, at rest.

items.statement: In twin studies of mostly light teen use, the twin who used cannabis lost clearly more IQ than the other.
items.why: No clear extra loss, though these studies could miss a small one. One study found about 6 points lost after years of dependence.

items.statement: In a UK expert ranking of 20 drugs, tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose.
items.why: Lung cancer was counted elsewhere, and the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined. The scores are one panel's views, not measures.

items.statement: Eye problems after poppers have only been reported after years of heavy use.
items.why: Reports from at least 12 countries include some people affected after using poppers once, though such reports cannot prove poppers were the cause.

items.statement: With MDMA, blood alcohol was a bit lower, yet people felt just as drunk.
items.why: 15% lower at its peak, in 9 men, but drunk ratings didn't fall, and test scores at their worst dropped about as much.

items.statement: One dose of meth leaves people sadder and craving it the next morning.
items.why: In one small lab study, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly the next morning than a dummy dose, but not sadder or more worried, and they didn't want meth more. Only eleven people took part, in a hospital unit.

items.statement: In studies, older people taking sleeping pills had more falls than those not taking them.
items.why: These studies watched what happened, so they cannot prove the pills caused the falls.

items.statement: In a lab study, caffeine made people who have it often more alert than people who rarely have it.
items.why: Caffeine only brought them up to the alertness of people who rarely have it. One study; people chose their own habits.

items.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with moclobemide or similar antidepressants as the riskiest mix they list.
items.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

items.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.
items.why: In one big online survey, about 2 in 1,000 people who'd used them in the past year said they had, and nearly all of those felt back to normal within a day. But nobody checked their answers, and anyone who couldn't answer wasn't counted.

items.statement: Studies show that starting to drink or use drugs young is what causes drug or drinking problems later.
items.why: Studies show a link but can't show starting young is the cause; much of the link runs in families.

items.statement: Most large studies found that women do worse than men once in treatment.
After Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use as a crime in 2001, drug use fell.
items.why: It rose slightly, from about 8 to 12 in 100 adults ever trying one. Treatment grew too, so the law's effect is unclear.

items.statement: Colour test kits for MDMA are easy to read, even for first-timers.
items.why: In one small 2003 lab study, two people new to the kit made many mistakes: one missed both MDMA samples, and the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right.

items.statement: Once a person has died, the level of a drug in their blood no longer changes.
items.why: Levels can rise or fall and differ between blood vessels, though these studies can't predict the change in one death.

items.statement: Most people who use meth end up diagnosed with psychosis.
items.why: In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record. No study has settled which comes first.

items.statement: Taking MDMA with alcohol makes you feel less drunk.
items.why: In a lab study of 9 men, MDMA took away alcohol's sleepiness, not the drunk feeling, and test scores still dropped.

items.statement: Most first responders in a New York survey said the news was their source on fentanyl.
items.why: Most named courses and training; about 1 in 7 named the news.

items.statement: In trials with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms or LSD made people's mood better than the dummies did.
items.why: Mood was not clearly better than with dummies, though people could feel a microdose on the day. Only one small trial used just magic mushrooms.

items.statement: Poison experts said a quick, accidental touch of fentanyl can easily make a police officer overdose.
items.why: They called it very unlikely, and no such overdose has been confirmed. But nobody has measured real touches, so it can't be ruled out.

items.statement: MDMA therapy for PTSD has been shown to work better than usual talking therapy.
items.why: Neither trial tested that: both compared MDMA plus therapy with a dummy pill plus the same therapy.

items.statement: A benzodiazepine sleeping pill at bedtime can't affect your driving the next day.
items.why: Some made people drive worse the next day than dummy pills did. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers.

items.statement: The warning against beta-blockers after cocaine is based on big trials.
items.why: It rests mainly on small lab studies, animal tests and expert opinion. No trial has tested beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine.

items.statement: Studies prove children's sleep gets better the longer they take ADHD stimulants like methylphenidate.
items.why: Not proven: in studies of longer use, the effect on the share of time in bed spent asleep only looked smaller.

items.statement: In a club study, people who took ecstasy felt sadder and less sociable two days later than other clubbers.
items.why: A week later they felt like the others again, but the study did not check what was in the pills.

items.statement: If a colour test shows MDMA, the pill has nothing else in it.
items.why: In one small 2003 lab study, seven MDMA samples that also held another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour as MDMA alone. A review adds that drugs close to MDMA, like MDA, give a similar colour.

items.statement: All fentanyl test strips work about the same, whatever the brand or batch.
items.why: In lab tests, one brand's 2021 batches needed ten times more fentanyl to show it than its 2017 batches.

items.statement: People who've quit ketamine do worse on memory tests than people who don't use it.
items.why: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well as people who don't use ketamine, and still did a year later. But most had used less than people who used most days, so this doesn't show stopping fixed anything.

items.statement: Long-term opioid use is linked with pauses in breathing during sleep.
items.why: Many people on methadone also sleep badly. This comes second-hand from a review that did not check study quality.

items.statement: Music has been shown to make ketamine treatment for depression work better.
items.why: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how well ketamine works. In a trial of 32 patients, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music, and the report gave no results on how sessions felt.

items.statement: An older study of people stopping cocaine at home described craving coming back after a few calm days.
items.why: In the closed unit, craving eased over weeks, but that place had no cocaine and nothing to remind the men.

items.statement: Two expert reviews that warn of seizures after stopping benzos suddenly say how often they happen.
items.why: Both warn the seizures can be life-threatening, but neither gives a rate. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners in 1961, in conditions unlike usual use.

items.statement: Among people who got ill after MDMA, low blood salt was more common in women than men.
items.why: In one poison-centre study, 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men. It counted only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.

items.statement: In 2024, a journal withdrew three MDMA therapy studies, saying the authors had not told it of serious rule-breaking at one site.
items.why: Most authors who answered disagreed with the withdrawals, and the journal did not say how much data came from that site.

items.statement: In most recent US overdose deaths involving meth, meth was the only drug.
items.why: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found fentanyl or other opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths. That's a different kind of record from the yearly death counts.

items.statement: Nitazene test strips pick up every kind of nitazene.
items.why: In a lab they showed 24 of 33 nitazenes, missing 6 of the 7 desnitazenes. Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested.

items.statement: It's been shown that psilocybin can change your personality.
items.why: Not proven. People rated themselves a little more open after, but the one test against another drug found no difference.

items.statement: No death has ever been linked to recent cannabis use.
items.why: A review collected 13 deaths linked to recent use, but 8 had significant heart disease or other illness, so cause is not settled.

items.statement: In a small MDMA study for depression, 4 to 6 of 12 people had worse thoughts of suicide at some point.
items.why: 4 to 6 of 12 had worse thoughts of suicide at some point, though depression fell a lot overall. No group went without MDMA.

items.statement: CBD reliably weakens the high from THC, the main active part of cannabis.
items.why: In most of 16 lab studies, adding CBD made no clear difference to feeling high. Most were small.

items.statement: People who use meth report much more low mood than people who use other drugs.
items.why: Against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference. Against people who don't use meth, low mood was somewhat more common, and things like a hard life may explain part of that.

items.statement: In US overdose deaths with signs of fake pills, most involved fake oxycodone.
items.why: In 2021 records, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30'. Death records likely miss many fake pills.

items.statement: In a survey, most festival-goers said sniffer dogs would stop them using drugs.
items.why: With dogs, 66 in 100 still said they'd use drugs, against 77 with no police. These were answers to made-up scenarios, not real behaviour.

items.statement: A US judge said the strictest ban on MDMA was not needed, but the drug agency imposed it anyway.
items.why: Before the 1985 ban, a few dozen US therapists used MDMA in therapy. This comes second-hand from one history review.

items.statement: In a London study, people who used ketamine most days more often felt cut off from themselves in daily life.
items.why: They also reported more unusual beliefs, mostly mild. Nobody was asked before they started, so the cause is not known.

items.statement: In studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often.
items.why: True, but only a link: studies of genes found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.

items.statement: Among people on prescribed opioids who died of overdose, half to three in four also had benzo prescriptions.
items.why: Half among US veterans and three in four in Ontario. A share of deaths does not measure risk.

items.statement: A negative benzodiazepine test strip means a drug has no newer benzodiazepines in it.
items.why: At one drug-checking service, strips missed 9 of 24 samples with newer benzodiazepines, and showed only 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.

items.statement: In a Swedish study, adoptive brothers and sisters, not related by birth, more often had drug problems when the adopted child did.
items.why: 6 in 100 did, against 3 in 100 when the child did not. The home a child grows up in is linked too.

items.statement: Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.
items.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

items.statement: In studies of stopping meth, people who don't use meth also scored better from retaking the tests.
items.why: People who stopped meth did not clearly improve more than them, in two small studies, so we don't know yet if thinking recovers.

items.statement: When people use cocaine with alcohol, the body makes a new substance, cocaethylene, that forms only when both are there.
items.why: Cocaethylene formed in two small hospital studies, never without alcohol. Neither measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.

items.statement: Taking MDMA with LSD pushes heart rate and blood pressure higher than LSD alone.
items.why: In a lab study of 24 people, they rose about as high as on MDMA alone. Body temperature wasn't clearly higher.

items.statement: In one study, violent crime was the crime most tied to months of meth use.
items.why: Among 469 people dependent on meth in Australia, the link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime, even after money and housing problems were counted. People reported use and crime for the same months, so it can't show which came first.

items.statement: Research shows most people feel a mid-week low a few days after taking ecstasy.
items.why: Two small studies disagree; the one that measured people a week before found no difference from people who use ecstasy but skipped it.

items.statement: Cannabis medicines work much better than a dummy medicine for long-lasting pain.
items.why: In combined trials, pain was only about half a point lower out of 10 than with a dummy medicine. The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.

items.statement: In one large study, most alcohol or drug poisoning deaths after leaving prison came in the first 4 weeks.
items.why: 91 in 100 came more than 4 weeks after release, though poisoning was also the most common recorded cause in the first week.

items.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.
items.why: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others: in one case of severe overheating, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat. That's second-hand, from one review of small studies and cases.

items.statement: Most people treated in hospital for alcohol withdrawal get the DTs (sudden confusion).
items.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 of them do, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. Most of these figures are passed on by that review or come from old trials.

items.statement: Teen cannabis use went up after US states made recreational cannabis legal.
items.why: Not in one big study of 1.4 million US high school answers: after recreational laws, teens were a bit less likely to say they'd used it in the past month. But only 7 states had surveys from before and after, and only for the first few years.

items.statement: In Ontario studies, gabapentin or pregabalin taken with opioid painkillers was linked to more opioid overdose deaths.
items.why: 12 in 100 people who died had a recent gabapentin prescription, against 7 in 100 similar living people. Reasons for prescribing were not given.

items.statement: The morning after heavy drinking, people remembered less and reacted more slowly than on alcohol-free days.
items.why: Memory and reaction tests were worse than on alcohol-free days. Studies were small, and a short night's sleep may explain part.

items.statement: With one benzodiazepine sleeping pill, flurazepam, next-day driving got slightly worse over a week of nightly use, not better.
items.why: Most pills' morning effect seemed to shrink over several nights, but not flurazepam's. Studies were small; none followed people beyond about two weeks.

items.statement: You can't die from opioid withdrawal.
items.why: Deaths have been reported, all in jail; one editorial suggests untreated vomiting and diarrhoea can dry the body out. How often it happens is unknown.

items.statement: Most people in treatment for cocaine say they've had paranoia or similar symptoms with it.
items.why: In a review of 17 studies, 68 in 100 said so, while strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100. Many also used alcohol or other drugs, so the review can't show cocaine alone caused it.

items.statement: In one study, sleep after stopping cocaine got better both on sleep-lab machines and in how people felt.
items.why: Machines showed people slept less and took longer to fall asleep, while their own ratings got better.

items.statement: Bladder problems linked to ketamine never ease, even after people stop using it.
items.why: In one survey, 128 of 251 people who described how their symptoms changed said they eased after stopping. No study has compared people who stopped with people who kept using, though.

items.statement: In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.
items.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

items.statement: In a Sydney study, most said they first took ketamine because friends did.
items.why: 62 in 100 said they first took it for its effect; 25 in 100 because friends did.

items.statement: Only people on DMT describe meeting a kind being that gives them a message.
items.why: Of 809 people who said they met 'God' without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind; 78 in 100 reported a message.

items.statement: People whose beliefs change after a trip start to believe in bad luck too.
items.why: In a survey of 1,606 such people, belief in bad luck from black cats didn't rise. Belief that plants can be conscious did, as they recalled it years later.

items.statement: Death rates were about the same in and out of methadone treatment.
items.why: In 16 groups of people on methadone, about 11 in 1,000 died each year in treatment, against about 36 out of it. People who leave differ in other ways, so this can't show cause.

items.statement: Most of 60 studies of ketamine for depression checked the bladder.
items.why: Only 5 of the 60 checked the bladder, and only 12 looked for side effects 2 weeks or more after the last dose.

items.statement: In one world model, the risk of every cancer it looked at rose with drinking.
items.why: The model's lowest-risk point balanced gains for some illnesses against losses; cancer risks still rose with drinking.

items.statement: The grumpiness and restlessness of quitting smoking usually last for months.
items.why: Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks, though for some people they lasted longer or came back. That comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

items.statement: Large amounts of meth or MDMA can make a fentanyl strip show fentanyl when there is none.
items.why: In the lab, meth or MDMA turned strips positive only at thousands of times the smallest fentanyl amount detected.

items.statement: Fentanyl test strips can miss some drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil.
items.why: In lab tests of 28 related drugs on four brands, three never showed up on any brand, and carfentanil showed only at high amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff.

items.statement: People whose depression lifted on esketamine relapsed more often when switched to a dummy spray.
items.why: Of those switched to a dummy spray, 45 in 100 relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The company behind it paid for the trials, and critics argue some relapses may be effects of stopping, which the trial couldn't tell apart.

items.statement: Six of the eleven authors of a big review of how ketamine works are named on a patent application for its breakdown products.
items.why: The idea that those breakdown products help in depression comes mostly from mouse studies by the review's own authors.

items.statement: The US government's anti-drug ads of 1999 to 2004 cut cannabis use among teens.
items.why: Teen cannabis use stayed flat (about 24 in 100 had ever used it), and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.

items.statement: In one survey of people who used ketamine, about 1 in 4 blamed it for urine problems.
items.why: About 1 in 4 did, in an online survey. But nobody who didn't use ketamine was asked, so the survey can't show ketamine caused it.

items.statement: Research shows crack cocaine itself directly causes the infections and violence linked to it.
items.why: The authors of a review of 302 studies say crack is not a likely direct cause of these.

items.statement: In a lab study, about a third of people rated themselves less 'open' after psilocybin.
items.why: On average, self-ratings rose by under 3 points, and the rise came from those who had a full mystical experience.

items.statement: In surveys, people who felt calm, open and ready the day before a psychedelic trip said it was less hard.
items.why: Surveys of about 200 people planning their own trip found this link; no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.

items.statement: The simple shapes people see on LSD have been sorted into just four types.
items.why: Lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals. Similar visions also come with flickering light or when falling asleep.

items.statement: The risk of dying is highest in the first week after leaving prison.
items.why: In death records of about 1.5 million people, days 2 to 7 after release carried about 1.5 to 2 times the risk of later weeks, and drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause. Tolerance was never measured, so the records can't say why.

items.statement: Studies of people given pure LSD found clearly more broken chromosomes.
items.why: In studies from 1967 to 1970, microscope tests found no clear rise. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.

items.statement: Six months after a trial, the psilocybin group was clearly less depressed than the group on the antidepressant escitalopram.
items.why: No clear difference: six months on, 37 in 100 on psilocybin and 34 on escitalopram were nearly free of symptoms, in one small trial.

items.statement: Crack and powder cocaine are two different drugs.
items.why: They are the same drug: crack is the form that can be smoked, and powder can't be smoked.

items.statement: If a breath test finds no alcohol left the morning after drinking, your driving is back to normal.
items.why: In a lab driving machine, young drivers with no alcohol left in their breath still drove worse than after alcohol-free nights. Sleep went unchecked.

items.statement: Mild signs of serotonin syndrome (too much serotonin activity) can look like ordinary drug effects.
items.why: The condition ranges from mild to severe, and doctors look for signs like muscle jerks and very brisk reflexes.

items.statement: In a UK expert ranking, alcohol scored worse than heroin or crack for the person using it.
items.why: False. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worse; alcohol came top overall mostly through harm to other people.

items.statement: In one small trial, caffeine pills around surgery meant fewer headaches afterwards for people who usually had lots of caffeine.
items.why: Fewer got headaches after surgery on caffeine pills than on dummy pills. Too small a trial to show the pills are safe for everyone.

items.statement: Fewer people went back to heavy drinking on naltrexone than on dummy pills.
items.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills; feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.

items.statement: When two officers felt ill after powder hit their faces, the lab found fentanyl in the seized drugs.
items.why: It found no fentanyl or other opioid, though a field test said fentanyl.

items.statement: In 5 studies, people who had stopped cocaine for more than about 5 months still scored clearly lower on memory tests.
items.why: Their scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

items.statement: In a London study, more people had taken ketamine at home than in clubs.
items.why: 71 in 100 had taken it at home and 84 in 100 at a friend's house; 52 in 100 in clubs.

items.statement: Alcohol before bed cuts dream sleep: it starts later and is shorter than on nights without alcohol.
items.why: In small sleep-lab studies, dream sleep started later and was shorter after drinking. Results were not the same in every study.

items.statement: In one US survey, alcohol use disorder was most common in people over 65.
items.why: It was most common at ages 18 to 29, at about 27 in 100.

items.statement: In studies of people of European descent, genes for drinking a bit less alcohol went with slightly less heart disease, not more.
items.why: These gene studies did not find that drinking a little protects the heart. They have possible biases of their own.

items.statement: Drinking alcohol was estimated to cause about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
items.why: A model put it at 741,000 new cancers, about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women, led by gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer. It's a computer estimate built on risks from studies of groups, not a count.

items.statement: Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.
items.why: Not shown either way: in one New Zealand study, people dependent on cannabis for years lost about 6 IQ points, but other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of mostly lighter teenage use found no clear extra loss, though they could miss a small one.

items.statement: Caffeine doesn't really change how much you sleep that night.
items.why: Across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same people, they slept about 45 minutes less after caffeine, and their sleep was lighter. These were healthy adults with low to moderate usual intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.

items.statement: The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.
items.why: In one big survey, more traditional practices went with a little more fear, and church hymns or sermons with less. The differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

items.statement: In lab studies, people who felt anxious and low just before MDMA felt more anxious than calm people did.
items.why: So did people who tend to worry. These were healthy young volunteers in a hospital, most trying MDMA for the first time.

items.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.
items.why: Across 7 countries from 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash. But most samples were seized by police, so they may not match what people buy.

items.statement: Meth seems to make nerve cells' chemical pumps run in reverse, pushing brain chemicals out.
items.why: It makes nerve cells let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. How is not fully known; this comes from a review.

items.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.
items.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples that had it. But trained lab staff did the tests, mostly with one brand, and testing at home wasn't studied.

items.statement: In studies linking ecstasy to lower memory scores, almost everyone also used other drugs, most often cannabis.
items.why: People who use ecstasy score lower on some tests, on average, but these studies cannot show ecstasy caused it; the gap may have come first.

items.statement: Rat Park has been repeated, with the same result.
items.why: Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result. In the original studies, the two groups also drank from different machines, measured differently, and all of it was in rats.

items.statement: Brain scans prove that meth kills dopamine nerve cells.
items.why: Scans show less of one dopamine protein in people who used heavily, but it can drop without nerve cells dying, and other markers aren't always lower. Experts disagree, and nobody has shown it either way.

items.statement: In the MDMA trial for PTSD that asked, most people could tell MDMA from the dummy pill.
items.why: 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right; neither trial reports measuring what people expected.

items.statement: Scans of people with vision problems after poppers mostly showed damaged light-sensing cells at the back of the eye.
items.why: People described blurry or dim vision in the middle; of those scanned again, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing. These are reports of about 113 people, so they can't prove poppers caused it or show how often it happens.

items.statement: MDMA therapy has even been tried, in a small trial, for ringing in the ears (tinnitus).
items.why: Reviews found single small trials for tinnitus and two kinds of anxiety. Outside PTSD, nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps.

items.statement: In older studies, headaches and sweating went up after people stopped smoking.
items.why: Tiredness, headaches and sweating did not rise; feeling grumpy, anxious or restless did. This comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

items.statement: A psychedelic flashback means reliving the whole trip for hours.
items.why: In Swiss lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, a flashback was usually a few seconds of changed seeing, mostly in the days after, and most people didn't mind it. These were healthy, screened volunteers, with no drug-free group to compare.

items.statement: Before training, most Indiana officers surveyed thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose.
items.why: About 4 in 5 did. Right after training, far fewer did, but only 69 of 204 answered both times; nobody untrained was compared.

items.statement: There is no such thing as cannabis withdrawal.
items.why: In general surveys, about 17 in 100 people who used regularly had it, such as irritability, poor sleep and low mood.

items.statement: In small MDMA trials, tiredness was common in the week after a session.
items.why: Five small trials gave MDMA to 58 people with conditions like anxiety or depression; a tight jaw, thirst and sweating were common during sessions, and none of the side effects were serious. The trials were too small to show rare or later harms.

items.statement: Children adopted away from a birth parent with a drug problem still have drug problems more often.
items.why: In a Swedish study, about 9 in 100 of them had one on record, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.

items.statement: More people finish opioid withdrawal treatment on buprenorphine than on clonidine or lofexidine.
items.why: In 14 trials, about 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on the other medicines, and withdrawal was milder on average. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

items.statement: There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.
items.why: Lists use different rules, some counting drug poisoning as the main cause and others drugs found in tests. In Norway, only about 49 in 100 deaths were on both of two lists, and in Sweden fewer than half.

items.statement: MDMA only raises body temperature when people dance in hot, crowded places.
items.why: Even resting in a room at about 23 degrees, 24 in 100 lab volunteers went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat, dancing and crowds weren't tested.

items.statement: Most men who used cannabis heavily never went to hospital with schizophrenia, in a big Swedish study.
items.why: About 38 in 1,000 men who'd used it more than 50 times later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who had never used it. These counts don't allow for other differences between the men.

items.statement: Regular cannabis use can come with bouts of severe vomiting that ended when people stopped, in most reported cases.
items.why: Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better. Nobody knows how common it is.

items.statement: In a small study, the biggest meth dose left heart rate and blood pressure higher the next morning than a dummy dose.
items.why: Next morning their heart beat faster and blood pressure was higher; but this was one small study of eleven people.

items.statement: In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in drug deaths overlapped with MDMA levels in deaths from injuries.
items.why: So a blood level cannot, on its own, show that a drug caused a death. An older review reports a similar overlap for morphine.

items.statement: A review says UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise.
items.why: In south-east London and Zurich, psychosis became more common in people born more recently; changes in diagnosis can blur trends.

items.statement: People who use ecstasy score worse on memory tests even if they use hardly any other drug.
items.why: In one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked that people used little else, memory scores didn't differ from others in the same all-night dance scene. Medium-sized differences couldn't be ruled out, and heavier use went with worse scores on one planning test.

items.statement: In studies, people felt more anxious and low when hungover from alcohol than when sober.
items.why: Most of 22 studies, with over 6,000 people, found worse mood when hungover. Poor sleep or regret may explain part.

items.statement: Parkinson's disease is common in people diagnosed with meth or amphetamine problems.
items.why: In Utah health records of people with such diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis, it was diagnosed about 3 times as often, but that's about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years, against 1 in 1,000. Some diagnoses were probably other movement conditions.

items.statement: In a US trial, one psilocybin session with therapists lowered depression scores more than a vitamin pill did.
items.why: Over 6 weeks, in 104 adults. But people could probably tell they had psilocybin, and nobody checked.

items.statement: People prescribed both opioids and benzos (calming medicines) had more overdoses than people on opioids alone.
items.why: Among US veterans, overdose deaths were about 3 in 1,000 a year with both, against under 1 without.

items.statement: In one study, men who drank alcohol heavily for years had fewer nerve cells in the brain's outer layer than other men.
items.why: Both groups had about 23 billion. But only the outer layer was counted, in 22 men; other areas were not.

items.statement: In one big trial, most people given naltrexone with bupropion had mostly meth-free urine tests.
items.why: About 1 in 7 did by the end, against about 1 in 40 on dummy medicines: about 1 extra person for every 9 treated.

items.statement: In a psilocybin trial for drinking problems, heavy drinking more than halved before anyone was given psilocybin.
items.why: It more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of talk therapy. Later, psilocybin was linked to fewer heavy-drinking days than a comparison pill.

items.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
items.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

items.statement: The most carefully run acamprosate trials found it clearly helped people stop drinking.
items.why: The most carefully run trials found no clear difference; overall, 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83.

items.statement: In one study, people off heavy cannabis use for a year or more scored like people who hadn't used.
items.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

items.statement: None of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis.
items.why: Two studies left out only people who had used cannabis recently. So these scans may mix up the effects of different drugs.

items.statement: In a trial with dummy capsules, microdosing magic mushrooms made people more creative.
items.why: Creativity tests showed no real gain in the week people took magic mushroom capsules, though they did feel something on the day.

items.statement: Adding MDMA to LSD has been shown to make a bad trip less likely.
items.why: In a lab study of 24 people in a calm hospital room, bad-feeling and fear scores weren't clearly lower than on LSD alone.

items.statement: In surveys, feeling safe and supported on a psychedelic trip went with far fewer difficult moments.
items.why: It went with fewer difficult moments, but only by small amounts, rated looking back. No study we read put people in different places on purpose.

items.statement: Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.
items.why: In a Swedish trial, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips. Everyone knew which treatment they got.

items.statement: The one study that watched real health care visits found worse care for patients with drug or alcohol problems.
items.why: It found better care for these patients, but it is one study from the 1980s; whether care is worse is not clear.

items.statement: Few people who go to harm reduction sites use drugs alone.
items.why: In a survey at 27 sites in British Columbia, about 3 in 4 had used alone at least once in the past week, most often because it was easier and more comfortable at home. It's one survey, of people already going to these sites.

items.statement: Even after overdose training, people missed some opioid overdoses on a written test.
items.why: They spotted about 7 of 9, against about 5 of 9 for people without training. It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked, so training may not be the reason.

items.statement: Drinking a little alcohol has been shown to protect the heart.
items.why: People who drank a little had less heart disease, but non-drinkers included people who stopped, perhaps through illness. Alcohol may not be why.

items.statement: In ketamine lab studies, hallucinations mostly meant seeing things that were not there.
items.why: In lab studies of healthy volunteers, what was scored as hallucinations was mostly real sights and sounds that seemed changed.

items.statement: The two UK deaths most linked to mephedrone in online news were later found to be from alcohol and methadone.
items.why: One study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.

items.statement: Once people stop using ecstasy, their test scores bounce back, research shows.
items.why: Nobody knows yet: in a few small studies, people who had stopped for at least 6 months scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used. But these compared different people, not the same people over time.

items.statement: At one drug-checking service, nobody who brought a sample with a newer benzodiazepine expected it to be there.
items.why: At one service, 24 of 159 lab-checked samples had a newer benzodiazepine, and most also had fentanyl.

items.statement: Official records name the drug involved in nearly every overdose death.
items.why: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an 'unspecified drug' code. The gaps differ by place and rules, and most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.

items.statement: On average, an alcoholic drink before bed helps people fall asleep faster.
items.why: On average, falling asleep took about the same time with or without alcohol, across 27 small sleep-lab studies.

items.statement: A study proved that Vancouver's site for injecting heroin and other drugs cut overdose deaths nearby.
items.why: Not proven: deaths nearby fell more than elsewhere, but nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.

items.statement: People who've used both say synthetic cannabis is as enjoyable as ordinary cannabis.
items.why: In a 2011 online survey of about a thousand people who'd used both, they reported much less enjoyment, more bad feelings and more fear of others, and most preferred ordinary cannabis. Nobody tested the products.

items.statement: Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with trying cannabis.
items.why: Evidence the other way round was weaker, and these studies looked only at ever trying cannabis, not daily use.

items.statement: Bad trips are fairly common among people who've used psychedelics.
items.why: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip, and 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life. That's one online survey of US adults looking back over their whole lives.

items.statement: Most men get harder erections on MDMA.
items.why: In one survey of 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker on MDMA and 8 said stronger. They were remembering past experiences, and nobody tested their pills.

items.statement: Before a training, most first responders surveyed in Missouri thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose.
items.why: Only about 1 in 5 rejected the idea before; about 5 in 6 did right after. But nobody untrained was compared, and there was no later check.

items.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.
items.why: After an hour in a sealed, smoky room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over the US government's workplace limit, and 12 tested positive at least once at a lower limit some private tests use. That was one small lab test, mostly in thick smoke, not everyday smoke.

items.statement: Children on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate had trouble falling asleep far more often than on a dummy pill.
items.why: Across 35 trials, it was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine, though who recorded it changed how big the gap looked. A drug company paid for the review.

items.statement: In lab tests, one brand of fentanyl test strip read positive with large amounts of vitamin C alone.
items.why: The same brand never showed carfentanil. Brands and batches differed, and each difference comes from one or two lab studies.

items.statement: Caffeine added time awake in the night, yet in five studies people did not report more time awake.
items.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made falling asleep slower and time awake longer; in five, people did not report more time awake.

items.statement: People who started using drugs at 13 or younger more often became dependent than later starters.
items.why: In a US survey of adults who'd used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 who started by 13 had been dependent, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. A big twin study found much of the link runs in families, so starting young isn't shown to be the cause.

items.statement: Worldwide, alcohol is estimated to cause millions of deaths a year.
items.why: Global models put it at about 2.3 to 2.8 million a year, against a world where no one drank, and at ages 15 to 49 it was the top risk factor in one study. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

items.statement: On average, people dependent on meth score far below the normal range on memory and thinking tests.
items.why: They score somewhat lower on average, and group averages are mostly still in the normal range.

items.statement: A UK study scanned people's brains over 30 years and saw them shrink as people drank more alcohol.
items.why: Each brain was scanned once, at the end. It found a link: people drinking more were more often rated as having a shrunken memory area.

items.statement: Starting to drink alcohol young has been shown to cause alcohol problems later in life.
items.why: Not known: some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both, such as behaviour problems. Few studies followed young people.

items.statement: In lab studies, 15 in 100 people later called their MDMA experience disappointing or bad.
items.why: Looking back, 15 in 100 called it disappointing or bad and 67 in 100 positive. They were healthy volunteers with researchers present.

items.statement: In the one study that followed people dependent on ecstasy, 93 in 100 were no longer dependent about three years later.
items.why: But that group was small, about 12 to 14 people by our count, and studies disagree on how many become dependent.

items.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.
items.why: A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. But for most the lift faded within weeks, and people can often tell they got ketamine, which may make it look bigger.

items.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single psilocybin session among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
items.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

items.statement: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, people also prescribed benzos died of poisoning more often.
items.why: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people a year with a benzo prescription, against 1 in 200 without, even though those on benzos stayed in treatment longer. The study didn't allow for mental health, alcohol or street drug use.

items.statement: People who sought help for heavy cocaine use said the crash after a binge usually ended within a few days.
items.why: It usually ended within a few days. This is what 30 people in treatment told doctors, with no comparison group.

items.statement: When testing at one festival showed a drug wasn't as sold, most people handed drugs over to be destroyed.
items.why: At an English festival, 30 of 45 people whose drug wasn't as sold handed drugs over, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched. That was one festival with chemists doing the testing, and people may have kept other drugs.

items.statement: In one twin study, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants.
items.why: It was 48 in 100 against 26 in 100, in Australian twins who grew up together. That's a link, not proof cannabis led on: shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain it.

items.statement: In one trial, people in meth treatment felt much less sad and worried whether they did exercise or health classes.
items.why: Both groups improved a lot and the exercise group only a little more; people knew their group, so hope may explain part.

items.statement: People who use fentanyl test strips have been shown to have fewer overdoses.
items.why: No one knows yet: one US study of 732 people found no clear difference over four weeks; it could not rule out fewer or more.

items.statement: In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.
items.why: Two or more of 11 signs of problem drinking in a year count, and about half the cases were mild. Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

items.statement: At a Vancouver supervised injection site offering a fentanyl check every visit, about 1 visit in 100 included one.
items.why: Strip use varied a lot between places, from 1 in 100 to 77 in 100, by people's reports or service records.

items.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
items.why: In two studies of people on methadone, tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete. Reviews add that tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, so the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.

items.statement: In a large trial, naltrexone plus talking therapy worked much better than either one alone.
items.why: Naltrexone with therapy did no better than either one alone in this one US trial.

items.statement: MDMA therapy papers left out side effects that their own trial records listed.
items.why: More than half of the less serious problems in the trial records never made it into the papers, and neither did 4 of 13 serious ones, all 4 in people on MDMA. Most studies also noted only problems people raised themselves.

items.statement: Benzos were listed in about 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017.
items.why: That's 21 in 100 death certificates, up from 9 in 1999, with benzos listed more often alongside prescription opioids or methadone than heroin or fentanyl. Records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths doesn't measure risk.

items.statement: In big US surveys, women who became dependent on alcohol got there faster than men did.
items.why: They got there about as fast as men. The idea that women get there faster came mostly from people in treatment.

items.statement: Most people can't tell LSD from psilocybin if not told which they got.
items.why: By the 28-person study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, though the trips were rated alike.

items.statement: In the largest trial, drug tests confirmed the antidepressant mirtazapine cut meth use.
items.why: People on mirtazapine said they used meth about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people on a dummy pill, but saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most kept using. Two small San Francisco trials did find fewer meth-positive urine tests.
