items.statement: In MDMA trials for PTSD, many people given a dummy pill plus therapy also no longer had PTSD.
items.why: 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill no longer had PTSD about 4 months later, against 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA. In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

items.statement: In a US survey, people who used LSD or mushrooms still had more mental health problems once other differences were counted.
items.why: Before counting, problems were about 2 to 3 times as common; after counting other drugs, risk-taking and stressful events, none of 20 was higher.

items.statement: A journal withdrew three earlier MDMA therapy studies over rule-breaking at one trial site.
items.why: The rule-breaking was at one site. In 2024 the US regulator also said no; whether MDMA itself helps PTSD is not settled.

items.statement: At first glance, people who used fentanyl test strips in the largest US study looked twice as likely to overdose.
items.why: They more often injected and used fentanyl. Once other differences were allowed for, overdose rates were not clearly different.

items.statement: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover than ordinary cannabis.
items.why: About a thousand people who had used both said synthetic cannabis made it harder to get on with things afterwards.

items.statement: In four groups who used cocaine, 4 to 8 times as many died as others of the same age and sex.
items.why: Yes, 4 to 8 times. But all groups injected, smoked crack daily, were in treatment or arrested; many also used heroin.

items.statement: In lab studies, about 1 in 11 volunteers reported a short flashback after LSD or psilocybin.
items.why: Of 142 healthy lab volunteers, 13 said they had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.

items.statement: The early studies that linked LSD to broken chromosomes ruled out other drugs.
items.why: They did not. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks as people who had taken LSD.

items.statement: In two studies linking strong cannabis to psychosis, researchers tested the cannabis people had used.
items.why: Nobody tested it: people named the type they had used after becoming ill, and strength came from police, European and national figures.

items.statement: Ecstasy has been shown to damage dopamine nerve cells in people.
items.why: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn because its animals got a different drug, and five human scan studies showed no clear dopamine change. But very little has been measured in people, so this doesn't show it's safe.

items.statement: In one psilocybin clinic study, about half of 19 patients said the music sometimes made things harder.
items.why: Almost all also said it helped at times. They were patients with hard-to-treat depression, in one small study.

items.statement: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in children with Dravet syndrome, a form of epilepsy.
items.why: Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children on it, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. But the maker ran both trials, in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up, and shop CBD wasn't tested.

items.statement: Heroin overdose deaths are almost always instant.
items.why: Many deaths took hours, and other people were often present, in older studies relayed by a review.

items.statement: Pills sold as ecstasy have nearly always held MDMA.
items.why: In European tests in 2009, as few as 19 in 100 pills held MDMA in one country. These were pills people chose to bring in.

items.statement: CBD products usually contain what their labels say.
items.why: In a 2016 US test of 84 CBD products sold online, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label, and about 1 in 5 also held THC. Shop products, or today's, may differ.

items.statement: Babies whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy went to newborn intensive care more often.
items.why: Across 19 studies, mostly from before 2000, these babies were also about 109 grams lighter. But many mothers also smoked or drank, and most studies couldn't tell that apart from cannabis.

items.statement: An SSRI antidepressant that dulls MDMA's effects also lowers MDMA levels in your blood.
items.why: In 12 men, the SSRI paroxetine lessened MDMA's rises in blood pressure, heart rate and pupil size, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 1 in 6 higher. Only healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most.

items.statement: Most people who start using cocaine are hooked within a year.
items.why: In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had used only powder were dependent within a year of starting, and about 22 in 100 of those who went on to crack. People answered once, so the surveys can't show crack itself made the difference.

items.statement: When MDMA is found in the blood of someone who died, it usually caused the death.
items.why: In 106 Australian coroners' cases with MDMA in the blood, 6 in 10 died of injuries, such as a crash. A blood test after death can't show who took what, when or why.

items.statement: With opioids, take-home fentanyl strips showed fentanyl about as often as staff tests on site.
items.why: In British Columbia, 90 in 100 take-home results on opioids showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site; with meth and cocaine, home strips showed it far more often, though the authors think most extra positives were false. The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.

items.statement: Only a few psychiatric medicines have been tested together with MDMA in studies.
items.why: Each was tested once, in 14 to 16 healthy people, and results differed: with MDMA, the antipsychotic haloperidol lowered well-being and raised anxiety. For several others, a 2022 review found no controlled study at all.

items.statement: People who use cocaine almost daily will always choose cocaine over any other reward.
items.why: In a lab, six people who smoked cocaine almost daily picked a $5 voucher over real cocaine about 1 time in 3 or 4.

items.statement: After cocaine, a beta-blocker improves blood flow to the heart.
items.why: In a lab test of 10 heart patients given cocaine, blood flow in the heart fell further in all 10 after the beta-blocker propranolol. None had used cocaine before, and what this means for heart attacks is unknown.

items.statement: In one study, more babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had birth defects than expected.
items.why: 12 of 78 babies born alive, about 15 in 100, had a birth defect, against the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and many pregnancies also involved other drugs.

items.statement: In a UK scan study, 35 in 100 people who barely drank had a memory area rated 'shrunken'.
items.why: 'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. People who drank more got the rating more often, but the study can't show alcohol caused it.

items.statement: Psychosis (losing touch with reality) linked to meth often comes back when people use again.
items.why: It often returns with renewed use; most of the studies reviewed were of hospital patients with meth psychosis.

items.statement: A medicine on sale today has been clearly shown to ease meth withdrawal.
items.why: None has; in nine small trials, only one drug clearly helped, and it is no longer sold. A benefit can't be ruled out.

items.statement: In one study, people who stayed to the end of a detox programme had fewer overdose deaths later.
items.why: The opposite: all 3 overdose deaths came among the 37 who finished it, and none among the 100 who left earlier. The researchers suspect lost tolerance, but nobody measured it.

items.statement: Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.
items.why: In a national survey, they were no less likely to start, fewer said they definitely wouldn't, and in one of three periods more ads went with more first use. The authors call that tentative, not definitive.

items.statement: Studies show people who drink a little live longer than people who never drank.
items.why: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths in people who drink a little, but compared with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or a small loss is still possible.

items.statement: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences.
items.why: Narrowly ahead of Salvia and LSD. Only the words were compared, not the experiences themselves.

items.statement: Levamisole, an animal worm medicine often found in cocaine around 2010, has been linked to blood and skin harm.
items.why: Case reports describe infection-fighting white blood cells falling very low, and painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin. But since most cocaine held it, finding it shows exposure, not that it caused the harm, and how often harm happens is unknown.

items.statement: In some US states, coroners, who are often elected, need no medical training.
items.why: Medical examiners are usually appointed doctors. Where coroners work, death certificates more often named no drug, but switching to examiners showed no clear change.

items.statement: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of a serotonin marker, in most studies.
items.why: Four studies found this link and two smaller ones didn't. But amounts came from memory, and people who take more ecstasy also take more of other drugs.

items.statement: In one estimate, about 25 in 100 pregnant women in the European region drank some alcohol.
items.why: Regional figures ran from under 1 to 25 in 100, mostly from a model, and the European region was highest.

items.statement: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
items.why: In questionnaires retold in one review, most said the first time was the strongest. But nobody checked what the tablets held, different people were compared rather than followed, and no lab study has tested it.

items.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis are a bit more likely to be depressed as young adults.
items.why: Across seven long-term studies, teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. That's a link, not proof: other differences between the teens may explain it.

items.statement: A death record can say morphine even when the person took heroin.
items.why: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine, and some death records named morphine or mixed drugs instead. In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than the records did.

items.statement: Caffeine can set off panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
items.why: In 10 small lab studies, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder had a panic attack after caffeine, and none were reported after a dummy. What ordinary, smaller servings do isn't known.

items.statement: Ketamine trip reports read more like near-death accounts than those for any other drug.
items.why: In one study, a computer compared the words in about 15,000 online reports on 165 drugs with 625 near-death accounts, and ketamine's came out closest, with salvia and LSD close behind. Only words were compared, though: nobody showed the experiences themselves feel alike.

items.statement: In one study, caffeine made people who often have it more alert than people who rarely do.
items.why: Caffeine only brought them up to the alertness of people who rarely have it. One study; people chose their own habits.

items.statement: In a 2017 kratom survey, about 4 in 10 people said they had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids.
items.why: 1,144 of 2,798 said so, and 849 reported 6 months or more off opioids. Nobody checked, and most were found through a pro-kratom group.

items.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.
items.why: In one study of ten healthy people, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self on the S form, while on the R form they described relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug, though.

items.statement: People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.
items.why: In trials, people guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they'd taken. Feeling an effect may have shaped that belief.

items.statement: In studies mostly from compulsory drug rehab centres in China, meth craving fell during and after exercise.
items.why: Craving fell compared with control groups, but these studies are known only through one weak review that gives no numbers.

items.statement: When a 2002 study on ecstasy and monkeys' brains was withdrawn, more big US newspapers reported the withdrawal than the study.
items.why: Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.

items.statement: In a US survey, most people who had ever had alcohol use disorder had looked for help.
items.why: Only about 20 in 100 who had ever had it said they looked for treatment or help.

items.statement: Ecstasy has been proven to cause lasting brain damage in people.
items.why: Experts disagree. Scans find less of a serotonin marker, but almost nobody was scanned before starting, so a difference may have come first.

items.statement: In a survey of almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, fasting went with less fear or fewer later problems.
items.why: Fasting showed no link the study could detect. Nothing was measured before people drank, and all differences were small.

items.statement: In a trial of 59 people, psilocybin clearly beat the antidepressant escitalopram on the main depression score.
items.why: No clear difference after 6 weeks (8 against 6 points), and the trial was too small to show psilocybin and escitalopram work equally well.

items.statement: Poison experts say fentanyl splashed into the eyes or mouth is no real risk.
items.why: They treat splashes into the eyes or mouth as a real risk, unlike a brief touch on the skin, which they call very unlikely to poison.

items.statement: Brain scans show that ketamine turns overall brain activity down.
items.why: In scans, brain activity went up, not down, most of all at the front.

items.statement: Buprenorphine helped far more people finish withdrawal treatment than slowly cutting down methadone.
items.why: They worked about the same: about 55 in 100 finished on buprenorphine and about 53 in 100 on methadone, in six small trials.

items.statement: Studies cited in a review say symptoms such as paranoia with cocaine usually pass after stopping.
items.why: Usually yes, but they can get worse with more use and last for weeks; most people studied were in treatment.

items.statement: Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, can also make xylazine test strips read positive.
items.why: In a lab, lidocaine also made xylazine strips read positive. Only one batch of strips was tested.

items.statement: Pills like Adderall give healthy people a big boost on thinking tests.
items.why: Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response. Daily use, studying and exams weren't tested.

items.statement: Meth poisoning can make the body get very hot.
items.why: Reviews of hospital studies list getting very hot among the signs of a body in overdrive.

items.statement: Studies have shown that benzodiazepines cause dementia.
items.why: Not shown. Quebec records linked long use to Alzheimer's; a Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

items.statement: In a big US trial, ketamine drips eased depression at least as much as ECT.
items.why: 55 in 100 on ketamine and 41 in 100 on ECT said their depression halved. But in Swedish hospital patients, more got well on ECT.

items.statement: Meth cravings go away as quickly as the other withdrawal symptoms.
items.why: In one small hospital-ward study, most symptoms eased within one to two weeks and low mood lasted about three, but craving lasted to week five, though weaker. The people in it weren't seeking treatment.

items.statement: Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths linked to it were in the news, one study found.
items.why: The author thinks the news raised interest, but search data cannot show the news made people use it.

items.statement: In a driving simulator, cannabis and alcohol together made lane weaving worse than either one alone.
items.why: A model of 18 adults' driving gave a 3.4 cm rise with both, against 1.3 and 2.1 alone.

items.statement: Kratom shows up in a large share of US overdose deaths.
items.why: In 27 US states in 2016–17, kratom was found in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths, about 6 in 1,000. Testing for kratom varied and wasn't recorded, so some deaths with it were probably missed.

items.statement: Passing out from GHB again and again has been linked to worse memory.
items.why: In one Dutch study, people who had passed out many times remembered worse than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs. It can't show GHB caused it, and nobody checked whether memory improves.

items.statement: The LSD chromosome scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish.
items.why: The cells came from just two people, plus a patient with no 'before' test; studies up to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. But those were small and looked only at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs.

items.statement: In a lab driving test soon after GHB, every person who finished crashed more than after a dummy drink.
items.why: In this lab driving-machine study of 16 adults, four threw up and could not finish; all the rest crashed more.

items.statement: The serotonin changes seen on scans of people who used ecstasy are known to be permanent.
items.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

items.statement: Eating poppy seeds can make you fail a sports drug test.
items.why: In a German study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake went over the sports limit of the time for morphine in their urine. But the cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, and workplace tests weren't studied.

items.statement: Overdoses were already falling years before Vancouver's injection site opened.
items.why: In the two papers critics cited, overdoses fell from the late 1990s on, and the site opened in 2003.

items.statement: Beliefs can shift after a psychedelic retreat and still be shifted 6 months on.
items.why: In one study, belief in things like other worlds rose a little and was still up 6 months on. But only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey, and most already leaned that way.

items.statement: Police officers have had confirmed overdoses from just touching fentanyl.
items.why: None has been confirmed: a federal safety agency looked into cases where officers felt ill and found no signs of a serious overdose, though no officer had a test that finds fentanyl. Finding no proven case isn't proof it never happens.

items.statement: Stopping regular cannabis use can mess with your sleep and bring strange dreams.
items.why: Between about a third and three quarters of people with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks, and in the lab they took longer to fall asleep. That's second-hand, from a review that didn't check how good the studies were.

items.statement: In one survey, most men who had used MDMA before sex said orgasm took longer.
items.why: 16 of 20 men said so, and 6 of 15 women, yet 32 of 35 people said they were more satisfied. It's one small survey of people remembering the past.

items.statement: Trials show cannabis medicines help with anxiety and depression.
items.why: Not shown: in the review we read, anxiety had only one or two small trials, and no trial treated depression.

items.statement: Indica and sativa labels tell you which smell compounds your weed has.
items.why: In 41,201 US lab-tested samples, the labels barely matched the mix of smell compounds (terpenes). The labels came from a strain website, not the bags, and effects weren't measured.

items.statement: In one small study, heart valve changes were more common in people who had taken MDMA for six months or more.
items.why: 8 of 29 met a definition of drug-related valve disease, against none of 29 students reporting no drug use. Nobody was scanned before taking MDMA.

items.statement: Brain scans prove that ecstasy destroys serotonin nerve cells.
items.why: Four teams found less of a serotonin marker in the outer brain of people who use ecstasy, but less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone. Nobody was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.

items.statement: The link between cannabis and car crashes stays just as strong when studies allow for drinking.
items.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

items.statement: In a UK expert ranking, alcohol came top mostly because of the harm it does to other people.
items.why: 46 of its 72 points were for harm to others. But the scores are one panel's views, and alcohol's score partly reflects how many people drink.

items.statement: Cannabis medicines have hardly any side effects.
items.why: In trials, about 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one, such as dizziness or dry mouth, against 62 in 100 on a dummy or another medicine, and more quit because of them. The trials were short, and long-term harms weren't studied.

items.statement: In three of five studies, people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol.
items.why: That was how people felt; measured on average, falling asleep took about the same time with or without alcohol.

items.statement: Psychosis linked to meth always clears up within a month of stopping.
items.why: In a typical study, about 1 in 4 people with meth psychosis still had symptoms over a month after stopping. Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.

items.statement: In 2024 the US regulator approved MDMA therapy for PTSD.
items.why: It said no. Its expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show the treatment works.

items.statement: In one trial, healthy adults' test scores rose after taking Adderall.
items.why: They rose on none of 13 tests, though people rated the Adderall pill as more helpful than a dummy pill.

items.statement: Cocaine with alcohol makes the heart beat faster than cocaine alone.
items.why: In 8 people on a hospital ward, heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both, against 74 with cocaine alone. These small studies didn't measure heart attacks or rhythm problems.

items.statement: In a big trial, ketamine treatment for depression caused more moderate or severe side effects than ECT.
items.why: Within 3 weeks, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect, against 32 in 100 on ECT. Across studies, headache and dizziness were most common, and most side effects soon passed.

items.statement: Drinking coffee raises your risk of lung cancer.
items.why: A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked: people who smoke tend to drink more coffee. These studies only watched people.

items.statement: By late 2021, about 15 in 100 overdose deaths in the western US showed signs of fake pills.
items.why: That was up from about 5 in 100 in mid-2019. Death records likely miss many fake pills, so the true share may be higher.

items.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.
items.why: Force, including sedation and electrical weapons as well as restraint, was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths among published cases. These were selected reports, so they can't tell how much restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused a death.

items.statement: A positive cannabis test shows that a driver was impaired.
items.why: It shows cannabis was in the body, not that the driver was impaired.

items.statement: In rats, heroin was more often deadly in a new place than in the usual one.
items.why: In one researcher's rat studies, yes. In people, it has only been looked at in 10 overdose survivors' memories, with nobody to compare them with.

items.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
items.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

items.statement: Given ketamine in one study, people with schizophrenia often described experiences that repeated their own illness.
items.why: These included suspicion, delusions and hallucinations. Nine patients in hospital, one study, and staff chose the order of the days.

items.statement: In the US, women with drug problems were much less likely than men to get treatment.
items.why: Reviews describe no difference: in 2015, about 10 in 100 women and 11 in 100 men who needed treatment got it.

items.statement: Confronting someone as a family works best to get them into treatment.
items.why: In one trial, 30 in 100 relatives started treatment after confrontation training, against 64 in 100 after CRAFT skills training. Seven in 10 families never held the confrontation.

items.statement: In a UK study, readers judged a man who died from drugs more harshly than a woman.
items.why: With story details picked at random, readers were also harsher when the story said heroin rather than ecstasy, or an older person with years of use. The differences were small to moderate, and readers answered straight after one made-up story.

items.statement: In one reported case, a man in a long breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP calmed in a dim, quiet room.
items.why: He calmed when put in a dim, quiet room; medicines for psychosis did not visibly help two of the men. Only three cases.

items.statement: In one small study, people slept about two hours less after the biggest meth dose than after a dummy dose.
items.why: A wrist monitor in 6 people showed this, and they also woke more than with any other dose.

items.statement: Around 2010, most cocaine tested by US drug police contained an animal worm medicine.
items.why: About 7 in 10 samples held levamisole. Case reports link it to blood and skin harm; how often it harms is unknown.
